title: Lincoln's House Divided Speech
speaker: Abraham Lincoln
before: On 16 June 1858 the Illinois Republican Party, meeting at the State Capitol in Springfield, nominated Abraham Lincoln for the United States Senate seat held by Stephen A. Douglas. That evening Lincoln, the only speaker, closed the convention. He argued that the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the Dred Scott decision were carrying slavery towards lawfulness in every state, and that Douglas's popular sovereignty would not stop it.
excerpt: "A house divided against itself cannot stand." I believe this government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free. I do not expect the Union to be dissolved—I do not expect the house to fall—but I do expect it will cease to be divided.
source: From Life and Works of Abraham Lincoln, edited by Marion Mills Miller (1907), as transcribed on Wikisource.
after: The speech was published in full at once, in newspapers, as a pamphlet and in the convention's proceedings. It opened Lincoln's campaign against Douglas, which reached its height in the Lincoln–Douglas debates; Lincoln lost the Senate race. When he published the debates for his presidential campaign of 1860, he put the House Divided speech at the head of the volume.
notes: The source line names the edition from the Wikisource page header (Life and Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Marion Mills Miller, 1907, scan-backed), which the importer strips: hence the checker's flags on 1907 and the editor's name. /wiki/A_house_divided redirects here; full uses the canonical title. Stephen A. Douglas, Dred Scott, the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the Lincoln-Douglas debates have no entries, so they stay unlinked.

title: John Brown's Last Speech to the Court
speaker: John Brown
before: In October 1859 the abolitionist John Brown led a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, meaning to arm enslaved people and start a liberation movement that would spread south; few joined him and he was captured. Tried at Charles Town for treason against the Commonwealth of Virginia, murder and inciting a slave insurrection, he was found guilty on all charges, and he spoke to the court when it sentenced him on 2 November.
excerpt: I believe that to have interfered as I have done—as I have always freely admitted I have done—in behalf of His despised poor, was not wrong, but right.
source: As W. E. B. Du Bois printed it in his biography John Brown (1909).
after: Brown was hanged at Charles Town on 2 December 1859, the first person executed for treason in the history of the United States. The trial, reported nationally by telegraph, turned him into a martyr for many in the North and a murderer in the eyes of the South, and the raid and the reaction to him deepened the divide that led to secession and the Civil War.
notes: Text from Du Bois, John Brown (1909), ch. 12, paragraphs 72-78 (the speech only; Du Bois's narration left out). The Wikisource page The World's Famous Orations/Volume 9/His Speech to the Court at His Trial (the target of the redirect John_Brown's_Last_Speech) was not used: its first sentence is garbled ("I believe that to have interference as I have done on behalf of his despite the poor was not wrong but right") and stands before "I deny everything". The articles differ on the date of the verdict (Brown article: found guilty on 2 November; raid article: sentenced on 2 November); before follows the raid article and Du Bois in putting the sentencing, and the speech, on 2 November. The Harpers Ferry raid and Henry Wise have no entries.

title: Itō Hirobumi's Rising Sun Speech
speaker: Itō Hirobumi
before: The Iwakura Mission, Japanese leaders, officials and students sent by the new Meiji government to study the West and to open talks on revising the unequal treaties, reached San Francisco on 15 January 1872. At a banquet the city's leading citizens gave the embassy, Itō Hirobumi, one of its four deputy ambassadors, answered the toast to the guests, reading his address in English.
excerpt: The red disk in the centre of our national flag shall no longer appear like a wafer over a sealed empire, but henceforth be in fact what it is designed to be, the noble emblem of the rising sun, moving onward and upward amid the enlightened nations of the world.
source: From The Japanese in America (1872), edited by Charles Lanman, in the OCR text of the scanned book.
after: The address was widely reported and became known as the "rising sun speech" (hinomaru enzetsu). The mission went on by rail to Washington, D.C., but failed to renegotiate the unequal treaties and sailed for Britain in August 1872. Itō later oversaw the drafting of the Meiji Constitution of 1889 and became Japan's first prime minister in 1885.
notes: No transcription exists on Wikisource or Gutenberg; the text is the Internet Archive OCR (djvu.txt) of the Google scan japaneseinameri01morigoog of Lanman, The Japanese in America (1872), the cleanest of three copies compared (japaneseinam00lanmrich drops end-of-line hyphens). Three source rows skip the running heads (paras 191 '14 THE JAPANESE IN AMERICA.' and 202 'HISTORY OF THE EMBASSY. 15'). BEFORE RELEASE the editor should add to $FIXES (ito-rising-sun), each matching once: 'ex- press' > 'express'; 'heart- felt' > 'heartfelt'; 'out- line' > 'outline'; 'instructibn' > 'instruction'; 'gener- ally' > 'generally'; 'oar maidens' > 'our maidens'; 'practi- cal' > 'practical'; 'stretch- ing' > 'stretching'; 'calcula- ted' > 'calculated'; 'privileges of our people.' > 'privileges of our people,' (the lanmrich copy has the comma); 'co operation' > 'co-operation'; '44 The red disk' > opening quote + 'The red disk' (the OCR read the quote mark as 44). And to $JOINS: the paragraph ending 'military, naval,' and the one ending 'privileges of our people,' (page breaks). Every paragraph opens with a quote mark, as the book quotes the address paragraph by paragraph. The excerpt is clean in the OCR as it stands. Date: the Ito article says 'In January 1872, at a welcoming event in San Francisco'; Lanman (para 179, outside the imported text) dates the banquet at the Grand Hotel to 23 January, which display uses. The brief said December 1871 or 1872: the mission sailed on 23 December 1871 and reached San Francisco on 15 January 1872. Lanman says Ito read the address in English; the Chief Ambassador (Iwakura) spoke before him in Japanese, his words read in English by an aide.

title: Elizabeth Cady Stanton: The Solitude of Self
speaker: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
before: In 1892 Elizabeth Cady Stanton was ending her term as the first president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, formed in 1890 when the two wings of the suffrage movement merged. She gave the address that became known as The Solitude of Self three times in as many days: twice to committees of Congress, among them the Committee of the Judiciary, and once as her last address to the association.
excerpt: And yet, there is a solitude, which each and every one of us has always carried with him, more inaccessible than the ice-cold mountains, more profound than the midnight sea; the solitude of self.
source: As transcribed on Wikisource, from the address to the Committee of the Judiciary; the transcription does not name the printed edition it follows.
after: At the 1892 convention Stanton declined re-election and Susan B. Anthony became president. Stanton considered the speech her best. She grew estranged from the suffrage movement after the association voted in 1896 to distance itself from her Woman's Bible, and died in New York City in October 1902, eighteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment gave American women the vote.
notes: Display is 1892, as the article gives it; the Wikisource header says the address was delivered before the Committee of the Judiciary of the United States Congress on Monday, 18 January 1892 (the text opens 'Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee'). The Wikisource page is marked 75% and names no printed source (slips such as 'My feelings was', 'youngwife', 'concience'): a scan-backed edition would be better if one turns up. The checker flags 'Wikisource' in source (not in the article).

title: Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Exposition Address
speaker: Booker T. Washington
before: Booker T. Washington, born into slavery and head of the Tuskegee Institute since 1881, spoke at the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta on 18 September 1895, introduced by the former governor of Georgia Rufus Bullock, to a segregated audience of black and white listeners. Southern states were passing laws that enforced segregation and kept black citizens from voting, and Frederick Douglass had died that February.
excerpt: In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.
source: From Washington's autobiography Up from Slavery (1901), in which he printed the address in full.
after: The white listeners gave him a standing ovation, the text went to newspapers across the country by telegraph, and President Grover Cleveland wrote to congratulate him. W. E. B. Du Bois named the bargain the "Atlanta Compromise" in 1903 and led the opposition to it, which formed the Niagara Movement in 1905, forerunner of the NAACP. Segregation was not ended, and Jim Crow laws spread across the South.
notes: Text from Up from Slavery (1901), ch. 14, paragraphs 4-16 (scan-backed), rather than the unsourced Wikisource page Atlanta_Compromise (which has 'extremist folly' for 'extremest folly'). Para 13 reads 'one-thirds its intelligence': perhaps a slip for 'one-third'; check the scan and add a $FIXES pair if so. Tuskegee Institute, the Cotton States Exposition and the Niagara Movement have no entries.
